cues.text: Healing an African and Eastern Rift
Sixtus II became pope in August 257, inheriting a bitter dispute left by his predecessor Stephen I over whether baptisms performed by heretical or schismatic clergy should be considered valid.
Where Stephen had clashed sharply with St. Cyprian of Carthage and much of the Eastern Church over this question, Sixtus worked with notable tact.
He restored friendly relations with both Africa and the East without abandoning the Roman position, easing tensions that had genuinely threatened to split the wider Church.
A Renewed Persecution
Emperor Valerian , who had at first tolerated Christian worship, issued an initial edict in 257 restricting Christian assembly and burial rites.
In August 258 he followed it with a far harsher decree ordering the immediate execution of bishops, priests, and deacons who refused to sacrifice to the Roman gods.
Sixtus, as bishop of Rome, was among its very first and most prominent targets.
Seized at the Altar

On 6 August 258 , imperial soldiers found Sixtus celebrating the liturgy in the cemetery of Praetextatus (by other accounts the Catacomb of Callistus), gathered with the faithful despite the evident danger.
Rather than flee and risk a massacre of those with him, Sixtus identified himself to the soldiers and was seized on the spot.
Four of his deacons — Januarius, Vincent, Magnus, and Stephen — were beheaded together with him.
Two other deacons, Felicissimus and Agapitus, were martyred shortly afterward.
St. Lawrence's Warning
Tradition holds that as Sixtus was being led away to execution, his own deacon St. Lawrence , distraught at being left behind, asked why his bishop was going to his death without him.

Sixtus is said to have told him he would follow within days — a prophecy fulfilled four days later when Lawrence himself was martyred, roasted on a gridiron, becoming one of the most celebrated martyrs of the entire Roman Church.
Burial and Memory
Sixtus was buried in the Crypt of the Popes within the Catacomb of Callistus.
Roughly a century later, Pope Damasus I composed a commemorative epitaph for his tomb.
It formed part of Damasus's larger project honoring Rome's early martyrs in verse.
Sixtus's name was later inserted into the Roman Canon of the Mass, where it is still recited among the ancient martyr-popes remembered at every celebration of the Eucharist.
Legacy
Sixtus II is remembered as a skilled peacemaker who healed a dangerous rift between Rome and the wider Church.
He is also one of Christian history’s most vivid examples of a bishop martyred while celebrating the sacred liturgy.
That death gave the early Roman Church one of its most treasured images of pastoral courage.
